judgments.forked_readings_summary: All four readings describe the SAME task with near-complete convergence: add 60-second single-flight in-memory caching (IMemoryCache fronted by a static SemaphoreSlim(1,1) with double-checked locking) to ONLY the SessionToken .NET service's ValidateToken path, keyed by a hash of the token (never the raw token), wrapping the cpsl_validateToken_v2 stored-proc call; cache the full result object so every existing result code is replayed identically on hit and miss; release the semaphore in a finally to avoid deadlock; cache is per-instance/non-distributed (up-to-60s staleness accepted); CreateToken is explicitly untouched; register AddMemoryCache in DI if absent; add tests for hit/miss/60s-expiry/concurrent-collapse-to-one-proc-call. SCOPE: full agreement — identical boundary (ValidateToken in, CreateToken out), identical mechanism, TTL, keying, and concurrency model. SURFACES: full agreement — all four name the same set (controller/endpoint unchanged, ValidateToken service method, data-access proc call, DI/composition root, cache + semaphore, token-hash derivation, result-code contract, test surface). BEHAVIOR: minor variation only on what gets cached on negative/error outcomes. #1 caches all proc result codes (valid/expired/revoked/not-found) but not thrown exceptions; #2 and #3 cache both positive and negative validation results for the full 60s (with #2 noting it would surface a conflict if revocation must propagate faster); #4 caches deterministic validation outcomes but explicitly excludes transient/infra-error codes (e.g. E1000) and thrown exceptions from caching. All four agree thrown exceptions are NOT cached. The only fine split is whether a transient error RESULT CODE is cacheable — an implementation nuance each raised as an explicit assumption, not a divergent task. All four also share identical structural assumptions: SessionToken lives in a separate consumer/migration repo (not this framework repo), a single shared (not per-key) SemaphoreSlim is intended, 60s = absolute (not sliding) expiration, SHA-256-style token hashing, and no eviction/size tuning in scope. Functionally interchangeable implementations.

All four readings describe the SAME task with near-complete agreement: add 60-second single-flight in-memory caching to ONLY the SessionToken .NET service's ValidateToken path, fronting the cpsl_validateToken_v2 stored-proc call with IMemoryCache + a static SemaphoreSlim(1,1) double-checked lock, keyed by a token-HASH (never the raw token), preserving all existing result codes byte-identically, per-instance (no distributed/Redis), leaving CreateToken completely untouched, with unit tests for hit/miss/expiry/single-flight. I verified the shared factual basis: grep found NO SessionToken C# source in this code-forge repo (only audit evidence, the spec-analyst agent, and the generation spec), and examples/generation-specs/dotnet-service.md does contain the exact `static SemaphoreSlim(1,1)` + IMemoryCache pattern all four cite — so all four correctly conclude the work targets an external consumer repo, not this framework repo.

SCOPE and SURFACES: full agreement. Same path (ValidateToken only), same mechanism, same modified surfaces (service method, data-access proc call, cache layer, DI/Program.cs AddMemoryCache, token-hash key derivation, preserved result-code contract). #1 and #4 additionally list the controller/endpoint, but explicitly as 'unchanged' — a presentation difference, not a scope expansion.

BEHAVIOR: minor variation on ONE point — what to cache on a non-success outcome. #2 and #3 cache both positive AND negative/expired/revoked results for the full 60s (flagging it as an assumption to surface if revocation must take effect faster). #4 caches ONLY successful proc executions, deliberately NOT caching transient/exception (E1000) outcomes. #1 sits between: caches all proc-returned result codes including error-results, but never caches thrown exceptions. This negative-result-caching policy is a real but narrow difference; it does not change the path, surfaces, TTL, key, or single-flight mechanism, and is partly reconcilable (all distinguish thrown exceptions / transient infra errors from deterministic validation outcomes). It is a policy nuance on one outcome class, not a different task.

All four readings describe the SAME task with no material fork. Unanimous core: add 60-second single-flight in-memory caching (IMemoryCache + static SemaphoreSlim(1,1) double-checked lock) to ONLY the SessionToken .NET service's ValidateToken path, wrapping the cpsl_validateToken_v2 stored-proc call; key by token-hash (never the raw token); register AddMemoryCache in DI if absent; release the semaphore in a finally; preserve every existing result code byte-identically on hit and miss; leave CreateToken completely uncached; cache is per-instance/in-process (no Redis/distributed, up-to-60s staleness accepted). All four name the identical surfaces (service/business layer, data-access proc call, DI/composition root, cache layer, concurrency-control semaphore, token-hash key derivation, result-code contract, tests; CreateToken explicitly out). All four name the identical test obligations (hit avoids 2nd proc call, single-flight collapses concurrent misses to one proc call, 60s expiry triggers refetch, result codes preserved). All four share the same environmental assumption (verified correct: SessionToken lives in a separate consumer repo, not this code-forge framework repo — grep found no ValidateToken/cpsl_validateToken_v2 service source here) and the same defaults (absolute not sliding expiration; SHA-256-ish hash if not pre-hashed; single global semaphore not per-key; no eviction tuning).

ONE minor behavioral variation — whether NEGATIVE/ERROR outcomes are cached: Readings 1, 2, and 3 say cache the FULL validation result for ALL result codes including expired/revoked/not-found (negatives cached same as positives for the full 60s), with #2 explicitly flagging it would SURFACE a conflict if revocation semantics demand sub-60s effect. Reading 4 draws a sub-distinction: cache deterministic validation outcomes (S/W/E codes) but explicitly does NOT cache transient/infra-exception outcomes (e.g. E1000 from a downstream failure) so they aren't pinned for 60s, and a thrown proc exception must propagate uncached. Readings 1 and 2 already align with #4 on the thrown-exception point (exceptions release the semaphore and are not cached) — the only genuine spread is whether a proc-RETURNED error code like E1000 counts as cacheable. This is a small edge-case nuance on the cache-unit boundary, not a different task: all four agree the deterministic valid/expired/revoked codes are cached and preserved, and all four agree thrown exceptions are not cached. No divergence on scope, surfaces, the single-flight mechanism, the 60s TTL, the token-hash keying, the CreateToken exclusion, or the per-instance constraint.
